Singapore's job-switching rate fell to 5.7% of employed residents in the year ending November 2026, continuing a gradual downtrend from its 2022 peak as hiring slowed and workers sought stability, according to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

Among full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 who changed jobs, about two-thirds, or 65.6%, saw their incomes rise after inflation, with most gains reaching at least 5%.

Over a longer five-year span from 2021 to 2026, roughly 67% of job switchers enjoyed higher real incomes compared with about 61% who stayed put, MOM's Ang Boon Heng said at the November 27 media briefing on the advance labour force report.

More than nine in ten switches over the past year were voluntary rather than caused by retrenchments. Among involuntary switchers, only around 58% saw wage gains versus about 67% of those who left voluntarily, so job stayers and involuntary movers were less likely to out-earn their previous roles.

Younger residents below 30, especially the 15-to-24 age group, cut switching most sharply and cited stability for staying. Older workers aged 50 and above switched least, with about half holding jobs of at least a decade.
items.title: Fewer Singapore Workers Changed Jobs in 2026, but Most Who Switched Earned More

visual.alt: Bar chart. Voluntary switchers (2025-2026) 67 %; Job stayers (2025-2026) 61 %.

items.summary:
The Ministry of Manpower reported on November 27 that Singapore's full-time employed residents saw their real median income rise by 2.2% in 2026, down from 4.1% the previous year.

Real income growth for workers at the 20th percentile slowed to 1.3%, compared with 3.6% a year earlier, indicating smaller gains for lower-wage earners.

The ministry said the slower pace partly reflected more cautious wage increases by firms and higher inflation, which it projected would rise around 2% in 2026 versus 0.9% in 2025.

The figures are preliminary because full-year 2026 inflation data is not yet available.

Despite weaker gains for lower-wage workers in 2026, the ministry noted their incomes have grown faster than median incomes over recent five- and 10-year periods, with continued support from progressive wage measures.
items.title: Singapore real incomes grew slower in 2026, with lower-wage workers gaining least

visual.alt: Bar chart. Median full-time employed residents (2026) 2.2 %; Median full-time employed residents (2025) 4.1 %; 20th percentile workers (2026) 1.3 %; 20th percentile workers (2025) 3.6 %.

items.summary:
The nexos.ai platform positions itself as an all-in-one enterprise AI adoption layer, centered on a single gateway that routes every large language model request through one unified point where budgets, policies, and audit trails are enforced.

According to the article, this same endpoint reaches 200+ leading AI models, letting teams adopt new models without locking into any single vendor. This figure is drawn from sponsored content by Marktechpost's Asif Razzaq, so it should be treated as a marketing claim rather than an independent verification.

The gateway performs three functions: governance and control over which teams can access which models; spend optimization through routing, caching, context compression, and real-time cost attribution down to the request level; and reliability via automatic fallbacks when a provider fails or slows.

On compliance, nexos.ai states it holds SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, and ISO 42001 certifications, is fully GDPR compliant, hosts its platform and most models in Europe with zero data retention, and does not use customer data to train AI unless the user allows it.

The article frames these claims as a response to two pressures: teams adopting AI independently across departments without shared visibility into spend, and the EU AI Act moving governance from policy documents into daily operations. These are editorial arguments rather than independent assessments of nexos.ai's capabilities.
items.title: nexos.ai Launches AI Gateway Supporting Over 200 Models With Governance Controls

visual.alt: Bar chart. 200+ leading AI models reachable through one endpoint 200; Access to 200+ models with no vendor lock-in 200.

items.summary:
Tencent has open-sourced DFly2, a speculative-decoding drafter that reuses its paired target model's sparse key-value cache and indexer selections instead of keeping its own draft memory. The approach targets natively sparse LLMs such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Tencent's Hy4 flash.

DFly2 is a 0.85B-parameter, 5-layer drafter shipped with the Hy4 flash model, per Tencent. It pairs each draft layer with one sparse attention layer in the target, sharing that layer's latent key-value cache and attending only to positions the target already selected via top-k sparsity.

Tencent reports higher draft acceptance than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark on all three targets across general benchmarks. The margin over the stronger baseline is 3.9% to 10.5% on general workloads, rising to 10.0% to 31.5% on long-context and agentic workloads up to 128K.

On end-to-end speedup under greedy decoding at concurrency 1, Tencent reports 2.97x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 2.36x on GLM-5.3-Flash, and 3.19x on Hy4 flash versus DSpark. Serving throughput gains on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at matched per-user decode speed reach up to 81% more on SWE-bench 64K.

The smallest reported gain is only 3.9% over same-recipe DSpark on Hy4 flash general tasks at temperature 0, according to Tencent. Separately, the announcement claims up to 4.2x faster decoding and about 30% higher throughput than same-recipe DSpark for Hy4 flash agentic tasks.

DFly2 ships inside tencent/Hy4-flash as a roughly 12B-active MoE with 1M context, served via vLLM's default DFly method or SGLang's DFLY algorithm. Tencent says the draft attends to at most about 2K keys per token and skips prefill entirely, adding only one last-layer hidden state in the transfer.

Removing a conventional 3-layer drafter cache lets the same memory pool hold 1.73x as many requests at 32K context length, per Tencent's paper Table 2. The method is trained with AngelSpec on a quick-start setup of one node with 8 GPUs (4 inference and 4 training).

All benchmark numbers are self-reported by Tencent, which retrains the DFlash and DSpark baselines on the same recipe. Serving tests reportedly used NVIDIA H20 GPUs via vLLM at TP8 per instance, whereas Hy4 flash's default vLLM recipe targets 8x H200.
items.title: Tencent Open-Sources DFly2, a Speculative-Decoding Drafter That Reuses the Target's Sparse KV Cache

visual.alt: Bar chart. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash SWE 64K 81 %; Hy4 flash general tasks, temp 0 -3.9 %; Long-context and agentic acceptance 10.5 %.

items.summary:
Historic king tides and a climate-amplified super El Niño drove record-high coastal flooding across Southern California during the Thanksgiving holiday week. In Los Angeles, the tide peaked at 8.19 feet above average low tide, tying last month's record, while La Jolla waves also broke records just after setting them.

Climatologist Daniel Swain attributed the elevated water levels to an overlap between king tides and the super El Niño rather than storms. Assistant professor Joseph Lucey-Renteria said conditions were expected to worsen in December before returning to similar levels, but noted residents had been spared large waves.

Residents responded with makeshift defenses as streets closed and businesses posted 'Closed' signs behind sand bags. Lara Mitry's Sunset Beach home escaped damage while her neighbor Jerry Cimmarusti set up close to 300 sand bags; in Naples, Long Beach, neighbors raised sea walls about two feet using plywood.

Long Beach had put a $125 million sea wall retrofit project on hold earlier this year after costs ballooned and an oil production decline created budget pressure. The project has resumed but is progressing slowly, leaving 90-year-old eroded walls further deteriorating with each tidal swing.
items.title: Southern California Coastal Communities Brace for Historic Thanksgiving Flooding

items.summary:
An Israeli team at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev says it has identified why reverse electrodialysis devices that harvest energy from river-sea salinity differences produce far less power than lab models predict. The study, published in PRX Energy and led by Prof. Yoav Green with Oren Lavi and Dr. Ramadan Abu-Rjal, treats the nanoscale membrane and its surrounding fluid chambers as a single electrical circuit.

The researchers found that resistance in the water on either side of the membrane lowers the current a device can deliver. Models that ignore these reservoirs overestimate harvestable power by several orders of magnitude, according to the paper. Prof. Green says his framework establishes a deterministic baseline and shows engineers should prioritize reducing reservoir resistance—such as placing electrodes close to the membrane—rather than searching for exotic materials.

The model also applies to other ion-moving devices, including seawater desalination membranes, nanopore sensors used in DNA sequencing, and living cell ion channels. French startup Sweetch Energy puts the untapped blue energy resource at nearly 30,000 TWh a year.
items.title: Israeli Study Explains Why Osmotic Power Devices Fall Short

items.summary:
Statnett, Norway's transmission system operator, paused new grid reservations for data centers on 9 November and will keep the halt until at least August 2027 while it sets functional requirements. The move coincides with a government licensing scheme that bars new crypto mining sites.

Data center operators have requested about 34 GW of grid capacity in Norway, well above national peak demand of roughly 25 GW. Only 0.8 GW is connected today; another 4.2 GW holds reserved capacity, 10.8 GW sits in the queue, and 18 GW remains at the inquiry stage.

About half of the queued projects seek power by end of 2028, but with no new reservations until August 2027 earliest and grid build-out still to follow, those dates appear out of reach for established operators and newcomers alike. Projects that already hold reserved capacity keep their place yet must still obtain approval before connecting.

Norway is not alone in tightening data center access; Great Britain, Germany and Denmark have all tightened connection rules since 2025 as grid operators replace first-come, first-served queues with requirements favoring projects showing progress. Satellite images show that about half of the 1.5 GW due in 2027-28 in Norway shows new construction, though a single project accounts for most of it.

Norway has six operating crypto data centers totaling about 0.2 GW combined; under the licensing scheme new sites are barred and existing ones cannot gain more grid capacity or face restrictions once transitional arrangements expire. Data center power use in the NO3 price area fell from late 2025 as one large site stopped mining before converting to AI, then is rising again.

Hydro supplies about 90% of Norway's power and decades of surplus have kept electricity prices low relative to most of Europe; that advantage is set to erode. Under normal hydrology, rising demand could cut net exports by 71%, from 14.3 terawatt-hours in 2027 to 4.1 TWh in 2030, and a dry year could make Norway a net importer with winter prices reaching about €290 per megawatt-hour.

The government wants the data center industry to help build gas power with carbon capture and storage and offshore wind, but both have long lead times. Until new supply arrives, the reservation pause gives Statnett more control over incoming demand and helps limit price risk for households and industry.
items.title: Norway Pauses Data Center Grid Reservations as Demand Surges Past Peak

Tata Projects has secured a turnkey Balance of Plant (BoP) contract to support a 1.6 GW ultra-supercritical thermal power project in central India, awarded by an unnamed integrated power utility.

The agreement covers the design, engineering, manufacturing, supply, construction, testing, erection, and commissioning of systems that back the main boiler-turbine-generator complex, including coal and biomass handling, water intake and treatment, fuel and ash management, cooling systems, and electrical evacuation infrastructure.

Environmental facilities such as a 275m triple-flue reinforced cement concrete chimney with emission monitoring are also part of the scope. BoP components make up an interconnected portion of thermal plants that require coordinated engineering, procurement, and construction to keep operations running reliably.

Tata Projects attributes its track record to more than 5 GW of previously delivered BoP and EPC projects, plus flue gas desulphurisation systems covering roughly 9 GW of thermal capacity across India using Wet Limestone and Sea Water processes. The company frames the award as a signal that customers trust its technical depth and execution capabilities.

President Rajiv Menon said large power projects demand seamless integration of multiple engineering interfaces into dependable operating assets, with an emphasis on safety, quality, engineering integration, and disciplined delivery.
items.title: Tata Projects Wins BoP Contract for 1.6 GW Thermal Power Plant

visual.alt: Bar chart. BoP and EPC projects delivered (GW) 5 gw; Flue gas desulphurisation capacity covered (GW) 9 gw.

Shares of several Tata group companies rose on Friday after a Bloomberg report said the Tata Trusts filed a lawsuit challenging Natarajan Chandrasekaran's reappointment as chairman of Tata Sons Pvt Ltd. The filing, according to people familiar with the matter quoted by Bloomberg, signals an escalating power struggle at the top of the $185-billion Indian conglomerate.

The stocks in focus included Tata Power Company Ltd, Tata Steel Ltd, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Ltd, Tata Consultancy Services Ltd (TCS), and Tata Chemicals Ltd. These companies are among others within the broader Tata group that drew attention following the reported legal action.
items.title: Tata Trusts Sues Tata Sons Over Natarajan Chandrasekaran Reappointment as Chairman

items.summary:
Apple's iPhone Air received a significant price cut during Reliance Digital's Black Friday sale 2026, bringing the slim device closer to the ₹90,000 price segment. The article is titled around an effective discount of ₹32,000 on this deal.

The 256GB variant was listed at nearly ₹1.2 lakh before the promotion and is now available with a direct discount of almost ₹25,000. This brings the base price down toward the lower end of Apple's premium iPhone range.

An additional bank offer stacks onto the direct discount to further reduce the effective purchase price, making this one of the more attractive iPhone deals during the ongoing sale.
items.title: iPhone Air gets ₹32,000 effective discount in Reliance Digital Black Friday sale 2026

items.summary:
Japan Tobacco's shares climbed Friday after reports that the company was considering partnering in a multibillion-dollar bid for British cigarette maker Imperial Brands, potentially one of the largest takeovers in tobacco history.

The report came a day after US group Altria said it was weighing an all-cash offer for Imperial and discussing acquiring part of its business with another party. Tokyo-based Japan Tobacco declined to comment on the speculation.

In morning trade Friday, Japan Tobacco shares rose 3.6 per cent, outperforming a 1 per cent gain in Japan's benchmark TOPIX index.

Shares of Imperial jumped 13.8 per cent Thursday after valuing itself at £25.90 billion ($34 billion), even though the company said it had not received an approach but its board would consider any proposal.

The deal speculation reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth as smoking rates fall and newer nicotine products have been hard to use to fully offset that decline. Imperial's portfolio includes established brands such as Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, sold in more than 100 markets.

BTIG analyst Owen Bennett said the deal would make sense for both Altria and Japan Tobacco and could be completed without affecting either company's credit ratings. He noted that a Japanese buyer of Imperial's US business should avoid antitrust issues given a combined value share of 14 per cent, smaller than those of Altria and British American Tobacco.

Jefferies analyst Andrei Andon-Ionita said the deal could turn Japan Tobacco into a sizeable, diversified third-place US competitor with cost synergy potential. The company has been expanding its cheaper-label US business.

Japan Tobacco recorded an $8.7 billion loss last week after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries when President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure this month.

Mitsubishi UFJ eSmart Securities chief strategist Tatsunori Kawai said that seizure will continue to impede any share gains for Japan Tobacco.
items.title: Japan Tobacco shares rise on Imperial Brands takeover speculation

items.summary:
Japan's core consumer prices in Tokyo rose 2.9% year-on-year in November, the fastest increase since July 2025 and the highest pace in 16 months, according to data released Friday.

The figure came in below the median market forecast of 3.0%, but still marked a rise from October's 2.6% gain and kept core inflation above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for three consecutive months.

Prices climbed across food, daily necessities and hotel charges even as government utility subsidies ended, with one economist attributing acceleration partly to rising energy prices linked to Middle East conflict.

The data strengthens expectations that the BOJ will raise rates at its policy meeting concluding Dec. 18, though a senior Sompo Institute Plus economist warned the bank could forgo a hike if instability over AI and chip demand persists.

A broader trend-inflation measure excluding volatile food and fuel prices rose 2.5% in November after October's 2.6% gain, with gains spreading across services such as public transportation and medical care.

JPMorgan Securities' Ayako Fujita said price momentum should stay broad-based into the first quarter of 2027, expecting inflationary pressure to widen further across food and services.

Short-term Japanese government bond yields edged higher on Friday as persistent inflation reinforced rate-hike expectations. Governor Kazuo Ueda is set to speak Monday on the likelihood and path of a December hike.

The BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after a June increase, then held rates steady in October while signaling readiness to continue hiking toward preventing excessive price acceleration.

A majority of analysts surveyed by Reuters expect a December rate hike followed by another by end-March, with many projecting a terminal rate around 1.75% or 2.0%.

Hawkish board member Naoki Tamura said the bank must respond quickly to inflation overshoot risks, while less conviction exists on how far tightening can go as energy and weak-yen pressures are expected to ease in the second half of next year.

Oxford Economics' Shigeto Nagai projects headline inflation slowing to 2% by late 2027, allowing a multi-year rate normalization that would reach a terminal policy rate of 1.75%.
items.title: Tokyo Core Inflation Hits 16-Month High, Strengthening Case for BOJ Rate Hike

visual.alt: Bar chart. Reuters analyst median 1.75 %; Reuters upper bound 2 %; Oxford Economics terminal rate 1.75 %; Oxford Economics headline inflation 2 %.

items.summary:
US tobacco company Altria announced on Thursday that it is considering a cash-only takeover bid for UK rival Imperial Brands, making the firm potentially the next British company to fall to a foreign acquirer.

Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until 5pm on 24 December to either announce a firm intention to make an offer or withdraw from talks entirely.

Altria also said it was in discussions with a third party about possibly acquiring part of Imperial Brands' business, which could result in the company being broken up. The announcement followed Bloomberg reporting that Japan Tobacco was separately evaluating its own potential acquisition of Imperial.

Imperial responded by stating it had received no approach or proposal from Altria or the referenced third party and expressed confidence in its strategy and trading while reserving the right to consider any future offer.
items.title: Altria Considering Cash Takeover Bid for Imperial Brands

items.summary:
Ofcom has announced a new code of practice requiring public service broadcaster streaming services, such as BBC iPlayer, to appear first among the nine icons on connected-TV app menus. The regulator says these services should be immediately visible and given an appropriate degree of prominence so audiences can find them without scrolling.

The proposed menu order is set out by Ofcom as BBC iPlayer, ITVX, Channel 4 player, Channel 5 player, S4C Clic and STV player, with positioning varying according to where the user is in the UK. The code also requires public service programmes to rank higher than other content on voice and text searches when they are the most relevant results.

Additional recommendations require PSB programming to be clearly attributed to its designated broadcaster so viewers can identify the content provider, plus accessibility improvements such as subtitles and audio description for disabled people. Ofcom introduced these measures under the 2024 Media Act, which modernised rules on making public service broadcasting easier to discover.

The code is not mandatory but Ofcom hopes it will be in place within 12 to 18 months. Platform providers that follow its recommendations would be treated as complying with relevant prominence and accessibility duties.
items.title: Ofcom proposes giving public service broadcasters top prominence on smart TV app menus

items.summary:
Net migration to the UK fell to its lowest level excluding the pandemic in nearly 30 years, driven by fewer non-EU arrivals amid tougher government measures.

The decline comes as populist parties have gained ground across Europe on anti-immigration sentiment, prompting governments to adopt stricter immigration policies.

The Home Secretary said the government had 'restored control' over migration and would now focus only on attracting high-skilled workers through tightened visa rules for students and employees.

Analysts cautioned about economic consequences: a center-left think tank executive warned that reindustrializing the UK depends on having access to essential workers, while a migration expert cautioned that sustained net emigration could strain public finances.
items.title: UK Net Migration Falls to Three-Decade Low

items.summary:
New Bank of England data projects that about 6.5 million homeowners will see their average monthly mortgage repayment jump by £100 when they roll off fixed-rate deals, according to the bank's Financial Stability Report.

That figure is more than double the £45-a-month increase estimated in July's report and reflects higher rates on new fixed mortgages since the Iran war began pushing up deal costs. The average two-year rate was 5.99% and the five-year rate 6%, per Moneyfacts, while a Bank of England official noted no signs of rising mortgage defaults.

About one million homeowners coming off sub-3% rates by end of next year will see an average £200 monthly increase, roughly half the rise seen during 2023 and 2024. Dawn Fazackerley-King, a Pilates instructor near Ipswich who refinanced from a 1.4% deal taken in January 2022 to a 5.69% loan, faces about £200 higher monthly costs.

The Bank warned households facing the hikes may need to cut discretionary spending or draw on savings as energy and other essential costs rise, with lower-income renters having less buffer.
items.title: Bank of England forecasts average £100 monthly mortgage payment rise for millions

items.summary:
The fight over why Poundland collapsed has become a blame game between US owner Gordon Brothers and the company's management team, with no one disputing that their insistence on being repaid most of £22.5m in debt blocked potential buyers.

Management accuse Gordon Brothers of strangling the business by restricting access to its own cash, leaving them unable to restock ahead of Christmas, while pointing to recent sales growth as proof a turnaround was possible. MPs joined the criticism, with Business Committee members accusing the firm of 'predatory capitalism' and 'asset stripping'.

Gordon Brothers dispute these characterisations, insisting they lent £85m over 17 months to keep the business alive—arguing it would have collapsed in June without them—and that most of the nearly £20m taken out was interest on that loan. They say sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when bought and could not offset a £100m cost-cutting programme.

The company also faced rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates like other retailers. Gordon Brothers argue none of the buyers—Martin Property Group offering £5m up front with balance deferred, or Xyra Holdings offering £12.5m up front but reportedly unable to pay—could meet their terms.

The chair of the Business Committee wants both sides back before them to establish what happened, while most observers think a full-business buyer is unlikely and a breakup now possible.
items.title: Poundland owners and management blame each other over its collapse

items.summary:
A contributor to The Free Press symposium 'What we are grateful for' reflects on theoretical breakthroughs since his 1962 birth, noting that while the Standard Model of particle physics emerged in the 1960s and 1970s, he considers the early 20th century more exciting for theory.

The contributor observes that a theory of quantum gravity remains elusive and that string theory appears increasingly unlikely over time. He also states that the fundamentals of economics have barely changed even as empirical knowledge has grown.

He expresses hope for new theories aided by both humans and machines, pointing to a recently released but unconfirmed theory of quantum gravity attributed to Ven Chandrasekaran and Astra.
items.title: Free Press Symposium Contributor Hopes for New Quantum Gravity Theory

items.summary:
At a high-level dialogue in Geneva marking 25 years since China joined the World Trade Organization, Li Chenggang, China's international trade representative and vice minister of commerce, said multilateralism is essential for addressing global challenges. He called on all parties to use WTO reform as an opportunity to strengthen the multilateral trading system and enhance its role in global economic governance.

Li reflected that China used accession to deepen domestic reform, noting that respecting international rules underpins integration into globalization while reforms tailored to national conditions turn opening-up opportunities into development gains. He stressed continued commitment to common development, citing unilateral full-coverage zero-tariff treatment granted to all African countries with which China has diplomatic relations and to least developed country partners.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala praised China's economic growth, poverty alleviation, technological innovation, and contributions since accession. She said the experience provides an example for other developing members seeking integration into the multilateral trading system and commended China's capacity-building assistance through South-South cooperation. Okonjo-Iweala expressed hope that China would continue to play a constructive role in WTO reform.

More than 200 participants attended the event, including ambassadors and deputy permanent representatives from major WTO members as well as representatives of international organizations, media outlets, and think tanks. Discussions covered China's achievements over the past quarter-century and ways to uphold the multilateral trading system and promote inclusive economic globalization.
items.title: China Reaffirms Commitment to WTO-Centered Multilateral Trading System

The inaugural China-Mongolia-Russia international passenger train (V3/4) from Beijing to Irkutsk arrived at Ulan Bator Railway Station on Thursday afternoon, marking the start of a new weekly cross-border service.

The route spans all three countries and covers about 2,666 kilometers over roughly 55 hours. Border inspection and immigration take place at designated crossings in China (Erenhot), Mongolia (Zamiin-Uud and Sukhbaatar), and Russia (Naushki).

Cao Li, chargé d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in Mongolia, said the service aims to boost cross-border trade, people-to-people ties, and the China-Mongolia-Russia Economic Corridor.

The round-trip runs weekly. Train V3 departs Beijing Railway Station every Wednesday at 7:27 a.m., while the return train V4 leaves Irkutsk Railway Station every Saturday at 6:58 a.m.
items.title: China-Mongolia-Russia passenger train arrives in Ulan Bator

items.summary:
A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce firmly opposed the United States' proposed additional Section 301 tariffs on China and other economies, calling them a unilateral act that violates World Trade Organization rules.

The Office of the US Trade Representative announced results from its Section 301 investigation into alleged overcapacity, proposing to impose additional Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies including China. The Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said this investigation is a typical example of unilateralism that disrupts the international economic order.

Spokesperson He Yadong argued the US was using 'overcapacity' as a pretext for protectionism, politicizing normal market competition and turning industrial development into political tools. He warned these practices would push up global inflation, harm businesses and consumers, and create long-term risks to global economic growth.
items.title: China Opposes New US Section 301 Tariffs on Overcapacity

items.summary:
A road accident left Pakistani patient Yasir Ali with multiple fractures that previously would have required a roughly 600-kilometer journey to Karachi, according to the report. The GDA Pak-China Friendship Hospital now allows patients in Makran, Balochistan, to receive surgery closer to home.

Yasir underwent treatment at the hospital and spent about seven days there before beginning recovery. Nearly two months later, he had returned to work.

The case is presented as an example of how China-Pakistan healthcare cooperation makes quality medical services more accessible to local communities.
items.title: Pak-China Friendship Hospital Provides Local Treatment for Balochistan Patient

items.summary:
A weekend of severe weather is forecast across Australia, including bushfires on Flinders Island, heavy rain and flooding in Tasmania and Victoria, storms across eastern states, and intense heatwaves in northern regions.

On Flinders Island, firefighters are battling an out-of-control bushfire that has destroyed or damaged at least eight buildings. The northern deputy regional chief of the Tasmania fire service, Steve Richardson, warned conditions would be hot and dry with winds up to 30km/h gusting to 50-60km/h.

Residents in several areas were told to take shelter after it became too late to leave, while others were advised not to return. An evacuation centre is open at the Furneaux Arts and Entertainment Centre.

The Bureau of Meteorology's Sarah Scully said heavy rain would hit northern Tasmania with six-hourly totals of 40-70mm and a risk of flash flooding early Saturday morning. Flood watches are in place for several coastal rivers, including Forth, Mersey, Meander, North Esk, Tamar, Ringarooma and the north coast.

In Victoria, rain began falling on Friday afternoon under a severe weather warning covering damaging winds from south-west to north-east. Six-hourly totals of 55-70mm were likely, with isolated falls up to 110mm possible and gusts up to 100km/h expected in the north-east Saturday morning.

Some parts of Victoria's Mallee and Wimmera had already received a month's worth of rain in about an hour. Yaapeet, a town of about 75 people in western Victoria, got 63mm in six hours including roughly 36mm in one hour, far exceeding the region's expected monthly total.

Victorians voting on Saturday could expect conditions to ease from mid-to-late morning, though showers and storms remained possible. Storms with heavy rain, damaging winds and large hail were forecast across eastern states from southern Queensland through northern and central NSW, including Canberra and Sydney.

By Sunday, the rain band and thunderstorms would shift into north-east New South Wales and south-east Queensland, including parts of Brisbane. Prolonged heatwaves in northern Australia were expected to intensify to severe or extreme levels in western Australia's Kimberley, with temperatures reaching the mid-40s, while Perth could see high 30s.

The article notes that global heating from fossil fuel burning has increased the frequency and severity of such extreme weather events.
items.title: Australia Braces for a Weekend of Extreme Weather, From Bushfires to Floods

items.summary:
Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the 'crime against humanity of murder' over killings that occurred between 2011 and 2019. Photographers who documented those deaths are reflecting on their work as his case proceeds.

Noel Celis, a freelance photographer who worked for AFP at the time, photographed about 200 drug war killings during the crackdown. He said he still reacts with fear when a motorcyclist pulls up beside him at a red light, describing the two-man teams that roamed Manila dealing out death as 'riding in tandem.'

Celis's most defining image showed a young woman cradling the bloody body of her boyfriend after he was gunned down at a busy intersection. To the mainly Catholic nation it resembled Michelangelo's La Pieta and quickly became the emblematic picture of the crackdown.

The journalists initially called themselves 'nightcrawlers,' named after a Hollywood film about Los Angeles camera crews chasing late-night mayhem. At first police had no problem alerting them to killings, but they stopped sharing information as public outcry grew, forcing photographers to chase mortuary vans summoned by police to collect the dead.

Dondi Tawatao, 46, recalled returning with AFP to a garbage-strewn street on a rainy night about 10 years ago where he photographed two bodies beneath the exposed roots of a banyan tree. He believed two handguns near them were planted there and described the scene as 'very dark' and sinister.

Tawatao said after shooting the drug war for four years, killings became so normalized that he stopped visiting crime scenes unless they involved at least three corpses. The long nights reshaped how he saw Manila, giving him a mental map of where people had been killed.

Kimberly dela Cruz, 36, found her first victim on Manila's rail tracks and another atop a major bridge. At the second scene she said the head of the man was wrapped in packaging tape next to a poster reading 'I'm a drug pusher, don't emulate me.'

Dela Cruz said some colleagues required professional counseling, with one suffering recurring nightmares about the dead coming back to life. She noted that residents of the mainly slum-area killing grounds could fear journalists as much as police.

Celis's memories centered on the keening of victims' wives and mothers and the sharp smell of blood. He said photographers wrestled with guilt over not being able to help and accusations of profiting from others' suffering.

When Celis and a colleague attended the wake of the La Pieta victim, they half-dreaded a lynching by angry relatives. They went partly to apologize for their inability to help and told the girlfriend that the pictures could serve as evidence if charges were ever brought.

Tawatao said all photographers interviewed believed the drug war did not solve the country's narcotics problem and remained convinced police murdered thousands to enforce Duterte's will. Celis added that Duterte 'ordered a war on drugs that killed many people' and called his death toll 'the natural consequence of his actions.'

Celis argued that photographs are powerful, especially now when he said standing history on its head is in vogue. Tawatao alluded to Holocaust deniers, saying the photos provided incontrovertible proof that the killings happened.

None of the photographers thought Duterte's arrest and handover to the ICC last year was possible until it occurred. Tawatao said he was shocked because they had only seen those in power get away with such acts. Dela Cruz described a huge sense of relief when Duterte was flown to The Hague, saying it meant some justice for families.
items.title: Photographers Reflect on Duterte Drug War as He Faces ICC Trial

items.summary:
The British Embassy in Tokyo is urging young British men to be cautious about a rise in drink-spiking incidents targeting foreign visitors across Japan. The embassy released its first post in a series this week, noting that recent spiking cases have focused on British men aged 20 to 30.

Drink-spiking refers to adding alcohol or drugs to someone's food or drink without their consent. According to data from the U.K.'s Foreign and Commonwealth Development Office (FCDO), spiking cases in Japan have risen by more than half over the past seven years, with male victims accounting for about 93% of those incidents.
items.title: British Embassy Warns Young Male Visitors of Drink-Spiking Risk in Tokyo

items.summary:
Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings said Thursday it would review its plan to complete an anti-terrorism facility for the No. 7 reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa nuclear power plant in Niigata Prefecture by August 2029.

The contracting company has informed Tepco that construction needs to be extended by more than a year because of factors including labor shortages, according to the power supplier. No revised completion target has been set.

This delay is expected to further push back the restart of the reactor after Tepco previously moved the facility's completion from October 2025.

An anti-terrorism facility also remains incomplete for the plant's No. 6 reactor, which was restarted in January this year and cannot continue operating unless that facility is finished by April 2031.
items.title: Tepco delays Niigata nuclear plant anti-terrorism facility completion

items.summary:
A jury has convicted former Queensland Royal Australian Air Force pilot Robert Crawford of the murder of his wife, Frances Crawford.

Frances Crawford died at her Upper Lockyer property in July 2024 after being discovered fatally injured near a toppled ride-on lawnmower. She was found trapped beneath the machine before she died.

Crawford pleaded not guilty and maintained that he had pulled his wife from under the approximately 200-kilogram lawnmower and tried to revive her, believing she may have died while moving it away from automated sprinklers during his sleep. Prosecutors alleged instead that he strangled her, manipulated her body and the scene, then called emergency services with a false account.

The jury heard testimony from more than 40 witnesses, including three defence experts, before deliberating for over three days to reach its verdict.
items.title: Former RAAF pilot Robert Crawford found guilty of murdering his wife

items.summary:
Premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has signed a two-year deal with the Papua New Guinea Chiefs to play in their inaugural season of the 2028 NRL campaign.

The 24-year-old Queenslander, who broke his relationship with the Sydney Roosters after the club's grand final victory, will head to Port Moresby following what he described as the best year of his career, which included State of Origin and Australian Test debuts.

PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters praised Walker's vision, kicking ability, creativity, game control, and experience performing at club, state, and international levels. He said Walker's partnership with Jarome Luai gives the team one of rugby league's most creative halves combinations.

General Manager of Football Michael Chammas said the Chiefs identified Walker as a player who could have a transformational impact on how they play and build their side. He described Walker as a premiership winner, Origin star, and World Cup winner whose best years are still ahead.

Walker is part of a wave of signings for the PNG Chiefs, who have attracted attention by offering tax-free contracts. In the past week alone, they signed Canberra and New South Wales backrower Hudson Young and North Queensland star Jeremiah Nanai.

Luai, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax, and Joseph Manu will also feature in the Chiefs' inaugural season. Walker is the ninth player the team has signed who holds either Test or Origin experience.
items.title: Sam Walker Signs Two-Year Deal With PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL Season

items.summary:
Sheikh Hasina has set 16 December as the date for her planned return to Bangladesh and said she is willing to walk across the border if no flight from Delhi can be arranged, putting Dhaka on edge while complicating relations with New Delhi.

Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule. She was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity in an absentia trial and faces arrest and execution if she returns; the UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the unrest.

The Bangladesh government insists Hasina must be extradited rather than allowed a voluntary homecoming, while India's foreign ministry said her extradition request is being examined through an established process. Analyst Avinash Paliwal argues Delhi has shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka and may not want to restrain Hasina or see the Awami League permanently excluded.

Hasina's aides say she has held more than 300 meetings with party workers across all 64 districts and 300 constituencies through her party's 78 units, and claims it could mobilise five million supporters in a human chain. Analysts caution that the Awami League remains banned and much of its leadership is abroad or jailed.

Awami League supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November according to Acled, with at least 11 people killed this month including two civilians. The party's ability to disrupt does not necessarily signal a broad political resurgence.

Many in Dhaka view the return as an attempt to test government authority and exploit divisions among parties that united against Hasina. Analyst Shafiqul Alam says the Awami League sees an opening amid disagreements over constitutional changes and a referendum, while analysts warn it could deepen hostility rather than revive the party's fortunes.

India-Bangladesh ties remain strained nearly 10 months into Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's tenure, with no visit to New Delhi yet. Dhaka alleges India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League but has not resolved extradition or renewed transit facilities for garment exporters as the Ganges water treaty nears expiry.

A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert warned December could be chaotic with protests and confrontation as the return date approaches, while Acled's Pearl Pandya said Hasina is unlikely to actually return given her death sentence. Paliwal argued India's least damaging outcome would be a fresh trial for Hasina alongside rehabilitation of the Awami League under new leadership.
items.title: Ousted Bangladesh leader sets return date as India faces diplomatic bind

items.summary:
Water companies in England will use government data to reach up to 250,000 vulnerable households who qualify for the WaterSure discount scheme. The Department for Work and Pensions will supply information on a quarter of a million households so water firms can contact them directly.

The £428 annual support is available to people on benefits who use large amounts of water due to medical needs or because their household has three or more children under 19. The government said 300,000 customers are signed up, but fewer than half of eligible households claim it.

The move follows criticism that too few people know about the discount and struggle to prove they qualify. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle called sharing information between government and water companies common sense, saying hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people miss out because they do not know how to access help.

Martin Lewis, founder of MoneySavingExpert, backed the change as a way for one part of the state to join up with another so entitled households are no longer left in the dark.
items.title: Water firms to identify vulnerable households eligible for discounts

items.summary:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told the BBC that delays in delivering anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and that the United States is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks. He said it was a pity America had focused its attention on the Middle East while withholding Patriot interceptors, adding that this deficit meant people's deaths.

Zelensky also criticized Trump for posting an image of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as 'my friend,' comparing calling Russia's leader a friend to being friends with Adolf Hitler during World War II. He described Putin as an aggressor and a killer who cannot be considered a friend, though he acknowledged the decision ultimately rests with the US president.

The latest round of peace talks mediated in Abu Dhabi made no obvious progress, with Zelensky saying 'the more we know, the more problems.' Talks are expected to resume in December. Trump said at his summit with Putin that Russia should pull back all military aggression and he believed a peace deal was possible, but Russia appears to have returned to hardline negotiating positions.

Zelensky called for real allies who can push Russia rather than remaining neutral toward the aggressor, arguing that neutrality supports both victims and the aggressor. The US argues it is staying neutral while searching for a lasting peace deal between the two sides.

Ukraine faces growing Russian strikes as civilian deaths reach an all-time high, with ballistic missiles targeting power stations and bridges and jet drones launched daily at Kyiv and other cities. Zelensky said Ukrainian forces can now destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones but face a very large deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles.

Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and its military version, Starshield, remain restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine, with drone units reporting they can no longer catch up with Russian Shahed drones. He said SpaceX makes the technical decision while he does not know who is responsible politically, describing it as a 'ping pong' between sides.

Ukraine increased long-range strikes on Russia recently, including an attack that sank the warship Merkury in eastern Libya. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni warned this could spread war to the Mediterranean and called it unacceptable, but Zelensky defended the strike as fair, saying Ukraine never attacks without coordinating with partners while accepting such moves are very dangerous.

Zelensky acknowledged a difficult winter ahead after Russian attacks targeted bridges over the Dnipro river in Kyiv. Some residents have left the city and businesses closed amid power cuts and strikes on logistics networks that have plunged much of it into darkness, but he said Ukraine will defend its capital because without one there is no country.
items.title: Zelensky Blames US for Missile Delays and Weak Pressure on Russia

items.summary:
Marine Le Pen condemned efforts to lock in the European Union budget before next year's French presidential election, calling it an 'underhanded' maneuver. The far-right leader voiced her opposition as EU leaders gathered at a summit meeting in Brussels on Thursday.

EU heads clashed over the bloc's long-term spending plans during talks where Germany is pushing for cuts and greater burden-sharing of funds allocated to Ukraine. European Council head Antonio Costa increased pressure on member states upon arriving at the budget negotiations, according to FRANCE 24 reporter Dave Keating reporting from Brussels.
items.title: Le Pen Criticizes Push to Finalize EU Budget Before French Election

items.summary:
The tenth edition of The Gingerbread City, unveiled on 26 November 2026, brings together 50 architectural models built from gingerbread and sugar.

Organised by the Museum of Architecture under its 'Future Forward' theme, the exhibition challenges architects to imagine buildings that adapt to climate change and improve wellbeing.

Among the highlights is a miniature Royal Albert Hall recreated with computer-aided design to capture the building's symmetry, alongside futuristic skyscrapers such as SpireHive, which explores living algae and self-healing concrete.

The show also features five structures inspired by homelessness experiences, created for charity St Mungo's by former Great British Bake Off contestant Carol Pui Man Li.

The exhibition opens to the public at Space House in Holborn on 28 November and runs until 3 January 2027.
items.title: London's Gingerbread City returns with 50 edible architectural creations

items.summary:
Farmers and tractor convoys staged a protest in central Brussels, marching past the European Parliament with banners demanding protection for agricultural funding.

Demonstrators warned that farm subsidies could fall by 20% under the EU's next long-term budget, according to farming unions cited in reports of the rally.

Lucas Bierlaire of the Walloon Farmers Federation said many growers were already struggling to make a decent living amid these pressures.
items.title: Belgian farmers rally in Brussels to defend EU agricultural subsidies

items.summary:
The tenth edition of The Gingerbread City, an exhibition of edible architectural models in London, was unveiled on 26 November 2026 and opens to the public at Space House in Holborn.

Organised by the Museum of Architecture, this year's show brings together 50 creations ranging from replicas of famous landmarks to futuristic skyscrapers. The exhibition runs until 3 January 2027.

This edition takes 'Future Forward' as its theme and challenges architects to imagine how buildings might adapt to climate change and improve people's wellbeing.
items.title: London's Gingerbread City returns with edible architectural creations

items.summary:
A letter from Ottoman sultan Mehmed IV to Spain's King Philip IV, dated April 1650 in Constantinople, provides evidence that official diplomatic communication existed between the two courts more than a century before such relations were traditionally believed to have begun.

The document offers an unusual episode in which the sultan proposed a peace and trade agreement with Spain similar to those already established with other European powers, including opening Istanbul's gates to Spanish merchants. Historian Rubén González Cuerva describes this as potentially 'a chance to change the history of the Mediterranean.'

González Cuerva leads a CSIC project on Spanish-Muslim diplomacy that prompted restoration, translation and material analysis of the letter after it had previously been studied in 2020 by researchers Jorge Fernández-Santos and Hüseyin Serdar Tabakoğlu.

The proposal may have aimed to break up an alliance between Venice and Spain during their war with the Ottomans. González Cuerva notes that even rival powers found room for negotiation, complicating the traditional narrative of perpetual conflict between Christian Spain and the Ottoman Empire.

An exhibition titled 'A Recovered Treasure: Arabic and Ottoman Letters from the National Historical Archive,' organized by CSIC's Institute of History and the archive, displays documents showing how contacts survived wars and religious divisions. Among them is a 1513 letter from the qadi of Tlemcen to Cardinal Cisneros.

The exhibition also features an exchange involving Lalla Fatima, wife of the Sultan of Morocco, who wrote in 1771 accompanying gifts with a request about Muslim women held in Spain.

Ottoman envoy Ahmed Agha spent time in Madrid between 1649 and 1650 posing as an extraordinary ambassador. Spanish authorities could not detect his true status because no one had accurately translated the letters revealing it, allowing him to live at the Crown's expense.

King Philip IV reportedly took amused interest in Agha's enthusiasm for bullfighting and theater, befriending some of Madrid's best-known actors and accompanying them on an excursion to El Escorial. González Cuerva recalls that 'to the king, Agha came across as a likeable character.'

González Cuerva argues that the idea of Spain as purely Catholic with no diplomatic relations with Muslims does not correspond to reality. The exhibition traces contacts from after the conquest of Granada in 1492 through discreet diplomacy between the 16th and 17th centuries, ending with normalized relations in the 18th century.
items.title: Ottoman Sultan's 1650 Letter Challenges Timeline of Spanish Diplomatic Relations

items.summary:
Farmers and tractor convoys gathered in central Brussels to demand protection for European Union farm funding, joining a summit where leaders are negotiating the bloc's next multiyear budget.

Demonstrators marched past the European Parliament with banners opposing subsidy cuts, including one machine displaying a placard reading 'Agriculture for sale, €0.'

Farming unions warn that agricultural subsidies could fall by 20% under the EU's next long-term budget, which would pressure rural incomes already strained by low farm earnings.

Lucas Bierlaire of the Walloon Farmers Federation said many growers are struggling to make a decent living as subsidy cuts loom.

The rally coincided with talks over the European Commission's proposed €2 trillion spending plan for 2028-2034, which unions say would substantially erode agricultural support in real terms.

Arnaud Rousseau of France's FNSEA union called on Brussels to show greater ambition for agriculture despite fiscal pressures ahead of a follow-up summit planned for mid-December.
items.title: Belgian farmers protest in Brussels to defend EU agricultural subsidies

items.summary:
The United Nations failed last weekend to open negotiations that could have led to a binding treaty banning autonomous weapons, also known as killer robots. Russia blocked the initiative under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which requires consensus to proceed.

Despite the setback, 163 of the 195 countries with voting rights had backed a U.N. General Assembly resolution last month calling for negotiations over an international instrument regulating these weapons. A single opposing vote stopped the process from moving forward.

Countries including the United States, Japan, South Korea, Germany, France and the United Kingdom also opposed signing a binding agreement on autonomous weapons.

Cordula Droege of the International Committee of the Red Cross said AI has been deployed prominently in conflicts across Gaza, Iran and Ukraine. She warned that systems with little or no human involvement could accelerate violence because humans would not be able to stop them in time.
items.title: UN Fails to Launch Talks on a Killer Robots Ban

items.summary:
Across several African countries, opposition leaders have accused authorities of restricting political freedoms through legal action and limits on public activity. Officials in each case say the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.

In Cameroon, organizers report that non-authorization of rallies is a major obstacle to campaigning. The law guarantees freedom of assembly but permits restrictions for public order or national security, requiring advance notification to officials.

Tanzania's opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026 the High Court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison. Prosecutors argued his remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election, while Lissu called the case political persecution.

Tanzania's chief government spokesperson Gerson Msigwa rejected allegations of repression ahead of the vote. He dismissed Amnesty International's characterization of a 'wave of terror' as unfounded and misleading.

In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience; he denies the allegations and says his statements ran against them.

Mozambique's Supreme Court judge counselor Pedro Sinai Nhatitima defended a decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide according to law.

In Nigeria, police in Borno State arrested five men wearing shirts with the slogan 'Tinubu Must Go!' The police said they were detained for suspected drugs and other items rather than political views; the men face charges including public disturbance and thuggery. In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting over public safety concerns.

In Zambia, courts closed on August 24 as the final day for filing an election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons while police said intelligence-led assessments were underway at several government institutions. State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema ordered the closure to prevent a challenge.

Former opposition lawmaker Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence in the same month. Authorities said officers came under gunfire and returned fire after intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat.

Zambia's Brian Mundubile faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures and has called for an open court process, insisting he is innocent of all allegations.

Constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde warned that public institutions are on trial. Cameroonian political analyst Kinang Derick Fai said democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.

DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.
items.title: Opposition Leaders Face Legal Pressure Across Africa

items.summary:
Vox, Spain's far-right party, is gaining support among young people as the country prepares for a snap election on November 29. The surge comes amid rising living costs and anti-immigrant sentiment that the party has used to broaden its base.

Recent polling from the Spanish Centre for Sociological Research shows about 23.2 percent of voters aged 18 to 24 support Vox, just above the roughly 22 percent backing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialists and well up from 15.4 percent in 2023.

Support has also risen among those aged 25 to 34, jumping from about 15 percent at the last election to around 22 percent by 2026 according to polls cited in the report.

For the first time since Franco's government ended in 1975, Vox could join Spain's government. The centre-right People's Party leads overall at roughly 31.5 percent and has not ruled out an alliance with Vox.

Political scientist Maria Elisa Alonso attributes the shift to a generation facing economic hardship without having lived through the dictatorship, making them receptive to narratives that blame immigrants for national problems.

Young Spaniards move out of their parents' homes around age 30 compared with about 26 in the rest of the EU. An average renter could pay roughly euro1,170 a month for a small Madrid apartment against an average gross salary of about euro2,460.

Vox blames immigration and crime for living costs after more than 70,000 migrants arrived in Ceuta from Morocco in late July. Its leader Santiago Abascal has called for 'remigration' and harsher penalties at rallies.

The party courts young men through social media content on patriotism and anti-feminist themes and imagery such as horseback riding and hunting gear. Around a quarter of male voters under 35 intend to vote for Vox, versus about 20 percent among women of the same age.

Vox has pledged to dismantle a 2004 law protecting violence victims and roll back LGBT rights established in a 2023 law. About half of young men aged 16 to 24 said in 2023 that equality policies had gone too far, Alonso noted.

Young voters are not uniform: hundreds of thousands have protested the housing crisis since late September and held a general strike on November 11 after an elderly woman's eviction. Some prioritize living conditions while others focus on national identity and want Vox in power.
items.title: Spain's far-right Vox is winning over young voters ahead of the November snap election

visual.alt: Bar chart. Voters aged 18-24, current 23.2 %; PSOE supporters (all ages) 22 %; Voters aged 18-24, in 2023 15.4 %; Ages 25-34, last election 15 %; Ages 25-34, in 2026 22 %.

items.summary:
US social media platform X introduced its first-ever parental controls on Thursday, November 26, enabling parents and guardians to manage the online experience of teenagers aged 13 to 17 while protecting their privacy. The feature allows parents to monitor screen time over a seven-day period, set daily limits, require approval for new followers, limit recommendations in the 'For You' feed, filter specific words, restrict sensitive content, control direct messages, and view which accounts teens have communicated with privately without seeing message contents.

The company stated that requiring follower approval also makes teenagers' accounts private. Both parents and teenagers must agree before supervision begins. Each parent or guardian can oversee up to five teenage accounts, while each teenager can be linked to only one adult at a time.

Parents cannot read private messages, access search or viewing histories, publish posts on behalf of their children, or log into the teen's account. Supervision automatically ends when a teenager turns 18, and all changes made through parental controls remain visible to the teenager. Michael O'Herlihy, X's head of safety, said parents want practical tools while teens deserve room to grow, adding that families can set guardrails fitting their home while teens keep ownership of their accounts.

The article is based on a company statement from X and does not include independent verification of these features.
items.title: X Launches First-Ever Parental Controls for Teen Accounts

items.summary:
IBM has discontinued H-1B visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of foreign workers in its US consulting business, reportedly giving affected employees three weeks to relocate abroad or resign by year's end. Those who leave will receive three months' severance pay with December 31 as their final working day, according to The Indian Express.

The company cited changing client requirements and shifting availability of skilled workers rather than attributing the decision directly to US immigration policy. In a statement quoted by The Indian Express, IBM said its participation in high-skilled visa programs had been declining for years as skill availability and client needs evolved.

The move comes amid broader tightening of US immigration under President Donald Trump's second term, which began in 2025. In October, the US suspended IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme that allows employers to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards.

Indians have made up a large share of recent visa recipients, comprising 71% of all H-1B visas issued in financial year 2023-'24. The Indian Express reported that IBM's decision is likely to impact several Indians.
items.title: IBM Ends Visa and Green Card Sponsorship for Most Consulting Workers

items.summary:
India's Parliament is set to hold a special session beginning November 30, with the delimitation bill as its central agenda item. This follows April's defeat of the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill by a united Opposition that denied the government a two-thirds majority. NDA managers now believe they may reach or approach the required threshold after an unprecedented churn in which lawmakers from several parties joined hands with the BJP.

Delhi's air quality was rated 'poor' at 8am Thursday, when the Central Pollution Control Board recorded an AQI of 220 and a 24-hour average of 224. Thirteen of 57 monitoring stations read 'very poor,' while 27 were in the 'poor' category and 17 moderate; Delhi Technological University logged the highest reading at 335, with Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium lowest at 130.

US President Donald Trump defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid national security scrutiny over China ties. Speaking from Mar-a-Lago, Trump said he did not consider Huang a threat and had enough information to support his view; AFP reported that Trump described Huang as happy about returning for what he calls his 'second term.'

The 2026 Fide World Chess Championship between Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh D produced its third consecutive draw on Thursday. The game lasted almost five hours over 60 moves, with Sindarov unusually holding position in his chair during the first hour.

Author Amish Tripathi defended Nitesh Tiwari's film 'Ramayana' for depicting Sita as a warrior who fights asuras and practices swordplay. In an interview with Screen, Tripathi noted that various versions of the Ramayana exist, including three attributed to Valmiki, one in which Valmiki also portrayed Sita slaying Ravana herself.
items.title: HT Morning News Brief for November 27

items.summary:
Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers with advanced AI chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the United States tightens export controls aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing restricted computing technology through overseas data centres.

The suspension follows a US Commerce Department interim final rule titled 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' which took effect on November 19. The rules add licensing requirements for exports of advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, countries Washington views as higher-risk diversion channels.

Manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro Computer reportedly told customers in the four Southeast Asian countries that Nvidia would not authorise their orders. The duration remains unclear because the move appears intended as a temporary measure while Nvidia and its partners assess compliance requirements under the new framework.

China is excluded from the suspension list because Washington already restricts direct exports of advanced processors to China through separate rules. The latest measures target a different problem: Chinese firms renting computing capacity remotely from data centres in third countries rather than buying chips directly, an arrangement that Southeast Asian operators have used to serve customers like Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance.

The suspension arrives amid scrutiny over Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an Nvidia partner under investigation for allegedly diverting advanced chips or servers containing them to China. The controversy also drew attention to Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive linked to someone connected with China's Ministry of State Security. US intelligence officials examined whether Chinese intelligence sought information from her.

Huang resigned before the board reinstated him as CEO on November 23 following intervention by President Donald Trump. Prosecutors have not established that she was directed to collect information about Huang or that she passed substantial intelligence value to China, and Beijing has rejected espionage allegations.

Nvidia executive Jay Puri's relationship with Cenly Chen, former chief growth officer at Super Micro Computer, also drew scrutiny after the couple married on March 7, 2026. The attention intensified following a Justice Department charge against Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan 'Wally' Liaw for conspiring to smuggle more than $500 million worth of servers containing Nvidia chips into China.

Prosecutors alleged that at least $510 million in equipment was diverted through a Southeast Asian company. Neither Puri nor Chen appeared in the indictment, and Super Micro maintained it was a victim while denying involvement in chip procurement.
items.title: Nvidia Halts AI Chip Shipments to Four Southeast Asian Countries Over China Diversion Risk

items.summary:
A report by Axis Bank Economic Research says the Reserve Bank of India may consider a sharper 50-basis-point repo rate hike at its upcoming December MPC meeting, though it keeps a 25 bps increase as the base case.

The bank cites resilient economic growth and persistent inflation as reasons for more aggressive tightening. It projects second-quarter GDP growth at 7.6% with gross value added rising 8.3%, driven by government spending, strong consumption, and easier working capital credit.

Inflation is expected to stay above the RBI's upper tolerance threshold of 6% until at least June 2027, according to the report. The bank also points to growing second-round effects as rising input costs increasingly pass through to goods and services prices.

Accelerating credit growth has been flagged as another sign of economic overheating in the analysis. If demand stays strong and inflation does not ease toward 5% in FY28, rates may need further increases that could push the terminal policy rate to about 6.5%, roughly 50 bps above the estimated neutral rate.

Interest rate swaps currently price in a 50 bps increase for December, reflecting expectations of tighter monetary conditions. The report suggests a larger hike would give the RBI room to pause later and reassess economic trends.
items.title: Axis Bank Report Points to Possible 50 Bps RBI Rate Hike in December

visual.alt: Bar chart. Q2 GDP growth % 7.6 %; GVA growth % 8.3 %; Inflation upper threshold % 6 %; Target inflation FY28 % 5 %; Terminal policy rate % 6.5 %; Projected bond yield % 7.5 %.

items.summary:
The Narendra Modi government appears ready to accept sweeping tariff and non-tariff concessions in exchange for a marginal improvement in its access to the American market, risking India's trade leverage as Washington pursues unilateral Section 301 tariffs. On November 25, US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer announced an intention to impose a 25 per cent tariff on Indian goods over alleged subsidies and excess capacity, while offering a reduction to 17 per cent if New Delhi agreed to what the article describes as a fair and reciprocal deal.

The proposed agreement would grant highly subsidised American agricultural exporters, pharmaceutical companies, and industrial producers zero-tariff or preferential access to India's market of about 1.4 billion people, including roughly 300 million classified as affordable middle class. The author argues that the one-percentage-point advantage Indian exporters might gain over competitors barely offsets the losses from opening this enormous domestic market.

India's response has been described as weak: New Delhi denied having structural excess capacity in any sector and insisted trade concerns be handled within ongoing negotiations, even though Brazil called for a WTO dispute panel against similar Section 301 tariffs. The article contrasts India's posture with that of the Modi government versus Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's administration, which reportedly said it would not bend to American tariff threats.

The piece also notes China accused Washington of political manipulation over its own higher combined tariffs and pointedly recalled a 2020 WTO panel ruling against US Section 301 tariffs that the United States then voided by blocking Appellate Body appointments. The author frames these measures as part of a pattern in which each expired or struck-down legal instrument is replaced, with IEEPA tariffs overturned by the Supreme Court and earlier Trade Act tariffs expiring.

The article concludes that India should weigh not just tariff reductions but the reciprocal concessions, surrendered market access, and lost policy space required for what it calls a MEGA deal at the G20 summit next month. The author warns that in its eagerness to strike an agreement with Washington, India may abandon multilateralism, reciprocity, and sovereign trade policymaking.
items.title: India May Concede Trade Leverage to Secure Tariff Reduction With Trump

items.summary:
A DC Edit opinion piece contends that the Trump administration's plan to raise tariffs on Indian goods signals gradual erosion of American economic supremacy rather than protecting it.

The proposed tariff increase would lift duties on Indian imports from 10 per cent to 25 per cent under Section 301, according to recommendations from the US Trade Representative (USTR).

These proposals emerged from a USTR investigation into the economic policies of 16 economies accused of creating structural excess manufacturing capacity that harms American commercial interests.

The article states these 16 economies and the United States together account for roughly three quarters of global economic output and more than two-thirds of international merchandise trade, though this figure is presented as a claim without sourcing.

USTR identified five alleged unfair practices in India: manufacturing subsidies, weak worker rights protection, capital allocation distortions, market access restrictions, and insufficient efforts to curb overcapacity linked to non-market economies like China. India rejected all allegations, asserting it has no structural excess capacity in any sector.

The editorial defends the government's right to impose tariffs as an exercise of economic sovereignty when domestic industries face threats or job losses.

However, the author disputes the core premise that higher import costs will restore US manufacturing and jobs, arguing countries like China and India have built sophisticated ecosystems beyond simple labor cost advantages.

The piece adds that any manufacturing returning to the United States may be increasingly automated, producing fewer jobs than expected.

As its central argument, the article emphasizes what it calls America's greatest structural advantage—the dollar's status as the world's principal reserve currency—which enables favorable borrowing and large deficits. The author claims steep tariffs on allies despite this privilege indicate that American economic dominance is fading.
items.title: An editorial argues Trump's India tariffs reveal a weakening US economy

items.summary:
The Centre has broadened its crackdown on Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation (IRF) by empowering state governments and Union Territory administrations to freeze funds and restrict access to properties linked to the organisation. The move follows a five-year ban extended by the home ministry days earlier.

A notification issued Thursday delegated these powers to states and UTs under Section 42 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, directing that all authorities exercisable by the Centre under Sections 7 and 8 of the UAPA shall also be exercised at the state level in relation to the banned association. The Central Government issued this direction.

The powers trace back to the home ministry's November 13 declaration of the IRF as an unlawful association, made under sub-sections (1) and (3) of Section 3 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, through notification S.O. 6182(E).

Section 7 empowers authorities to prohibit use of funds belonging to a declared unlawful association by issuing written orders barring anyone holding money, securities or credits from paying, transferring or otherwise dealing with them without government permission.

A gazetted officer authorised under Section 7 can inspect premises, examine records and investigate financial transactions suspected of being linked to the organisation. Section 8 lets authorities notify any place believed to be used for an unlawful association.

After such a notification, the district magistrate may prepare an inventory of movable property at the premises and restrict entry by people who were not residents when the order was issued. Police officers of at least sub-inspector rank can search individuals entering or found there.
items.title: Centre expands powers over states and UTs in crackdown on Zakir Naik's IRF

Swapan 'Babun' Banerjee, younger brother of former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and uncle of TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee, approached police on Thursday seeking registration of an FIR against his nephew over alleged threats and obstruction to a blood donation camp, according to news agency PTI. The complaint was filed at the Kalighat police station.

Babun said he had witnessed intimidation during the TMC's 15-year rule in West Bengal and that such incidents continued after the BJP came to power in May this year, claiming to have observed them since 2024. He cited obstruction of government work, forcible takeover of clubs, and intimidation as examples.

Details of the blood donation camp incident and the specific allegations against Abhishek Banerjee were not immediately available at the time of reporting. The complaint comes amid a long-standing estrangement between Babun and Mamata, who had previously declared that she severed ties with him.

The family discord has taken on political dimensions following the BJP's victory in West Bengal assembly elections, which ended the TMC's uninterrupted 15-year rule. Since the change of government, Babun has grown closer to BJP leadership and repeatedly praised chief minister Suvendu Adhikari.

Babun recently invited Suvendu Adhikari to inaugurate a community Durga Puja in his neighbourhood and was seen touching the chief minister's feet during the event. His repeated public admiration for Suvendu has fuelled speculation about his political leanings and possible shift toward the BJP, though Babun has not made any formal announcement of joining the party.
items.title: Mamata Banerjee's Brother Seeks FIR Against Nephew Abhishek Over Alleged Threats

The Allahabad High Court remarked that the legislature may consider reducing the age of juvenility from 18 years to 16 years, following a similar observation by the Kerala High Court.

Justice Abdul Shahid made the remark while dismissing a juvenile's appeal against rejection of his second bail application in a dacoity-murder case. The order was dated November 17.

The Kerala High Court had earlier observed that it is high time for legislatures to amend statutes dealing with juveniles and children in conflict with law, noting the present trend showing sufficient maturity among children at age 16.

Justice Shahid said this aspect may be duly considered by the legislature after taking note of the Kerala court's observations about maturity attained by children upon reaching 16 years.
items.title: Allahabad High Court says legislature may lower juvenile age to 16
